solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Well-informed jail's own source of monkey business

parts.note: to bang up is British slang for locking someone in a cell
on one's tod is British slang for on one's own, from rhyming slang Tod Sloan
Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and folly, the origin of rash misdeeds

explanation.surface: A prison's own supplier of shenanigans is remarkably well briefed on the latest goings-on.
explanation.walkthrough: BANG UP is British slang for lock up; TOD comes from 'on your tod', meaning on your own; ATE is the Greek goddess of mischief.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fully current with the latest news and developments is well-informed, an idiomatic synonym.

clue.text: Great Depression in the Seven Stars

parts.note: great means big
a depression or hollow is a dip
per means in the, as in miles per hour

explanation.surface: The economic slump of the 1930s seems somehow located among a group of stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great Depression' looks like the 1930s slump, and 'in the' gives PER as in 'miles per hour'. The Plough's seven stars are an asterism rather than a full constellation.
explanation.definitionFit: The seven brightest stars of Ursa Major form the pattern Americans call the Dipper and Britons the Plough.

clue.text: The world only dreamed of the judgment on the Flying Dutchman?

definitions.meaning: an imaginary ideal place, like Peter Pan's island, exists only in dreams

definitions.text: the judgment on the Flying Dutchman?
definitions.meaning: the ghost ship's curse is that it may ..., ever come ashore, so the sentence passed is '...'

explanation.surface: A legendary curse on a phantom ship is described as something the world could only imagine.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer into a sentence: the doomed captain will never, never land.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie's dream island is the classic imaginary place, a byword for a fantasy realm.

clue.text: Number one stunted Prince missed out — it is to be collected

indicators.note: is to be collected says the little word is gathered into what remains
missed out says the letter for the royal is dropped from the word

parts.note: something stunted is puny

explanation.surface: A short prince who was passed over is waiting to be picked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missed out' removes the royal letter, leaving UNY, and 'is to be collected' gathers the little word into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Unity is the mathematical term for the number one, a technical synonym.

clue.text: It's proved right — They Do It With Mirrors? …

definitions.meaning: a legal document that proves a right of ownership to land
this Agatha Christie novel's name is a title, and doing it is a deed, so the phrase is a title describing a deed

explanation.surface: An Agatha Christie mystery is hailed as having been vindicated, the trick done with mirrors.
explanation.walkthrough: They Do It With Mirrors is a Miss Marple novel; it is a title, and the 'doing it' is a deed. The ellipsis runs on into 5/24.
explanation.definitionFit: A property document proving ownership establishes the holder's right to it.

clue.text: … in which Marple eyes OTT verdict with suspicion

indicators.note: the letters are looked at askance, treated as suspect and rearranged

explanation.surface: Miss Marple regards an over-the-top jury verdict with distrust.
explanation.walkthrough: Continuing from 4, this is the kind of book in which Marple appears; 'with suspicion' rearranges EYES OTT VERDICT.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss Marple is Agatha Christie's sleuth, so the books she appears in are crime mysteries.

clue.text: One's often referred to as 'jolly' in this amount of heat

parts.note: this is a demonstrative standing for the definite article
a Royal Marine is nicknamed a jolly, and RM is the abbreviation for the Royal Marines

explanation.surface: Someone is called jolly when it is this warm.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'a jolly is what one is called in THE RM': Royal Marines are nicknamed jollies in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A therm is a British unit of heat energy, 100,000 BTU, used to bill gas.

clue.text: Its owner obsesses about right food in 60-second date

indicators.note: in says that combination sits inside the sixty-second phrase

parts.note: sixty seconds is one minute, ONE MIN

indicators.note: about says the food word goes around the letter for right

parts.note: tack is food, as in hard tack, ship's biscuit

explanation.surface: An obsessive frets over getting the right food on a speed date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the food round the letter for right, making TRACK, and 'in' sets that inside the minute phrase; 'Its owner obsesses' defines by describing who has one.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with this fixation thinks about one subject only, so its possessor is obsessive.

clue.text: Arid area of Mojave, generally to the west

indicators.note: to the west says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A dry region found in the Mojave, broadly speaking toward the west.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, westward is right to left, so VEGEN in 'Mojave, generally' is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Negev is a desert in southern Israel, an example of a dry region.

clue.text: Foremost of toymakers admitted new train-set's ruined

indicators.note: admitted says the picked letter is let into the rearranged letters
new says the letters of the toy are made afresh in another order
foremost of picks the leading letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A toy train set taken in by the leading toymaker turns out to be wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges TRAINSET, and T from 'Foremost of toymakers' is 'admitted' into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something torn to shreds or in ruins is said, idiomatically, to be in rags and pieces.

clue.text: Peers, say, after what comes fifth from the top in Debrett's?

indicators.note: after says the first piece is followed by the second

parts.words: what comes fifth from the top in Debrett's?
parts.note: the fifth letter of Debrett's is its second E, so the phrase gives SECOND E
to say is to state

explanation.surface: Members of the House of Lords rank, say, just behind the fifth entry in the peerage guide.
explanation.walkthrough: Debrett's is the British guide to the peerage, which makes 'fifth from the top' look like a ranking; it is just a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The nobility, the Lords temporal, formed the historic estate ranking after the clergy.

clue.text: When's the train due? Sooner Or later, for Spooner. And me?

indicators.note: for Spooner says the starting sounds of the two words are swapped, as Reverend Spooner did

parts.note: a train runs by rail
when asks for a time

explanation.surface: A rhyming exchange about when a train arrives, with Spooner chipping in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When's the train due?' is rail time; swapped by Spooner it becomes 'tail rime'. 'And me?' asks what the clue itself is: its short rhymed lines are an example of the form.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue's own verse, with short lines rhyming at the ends, exemplifies this stanza form.

clue.text: Sharing PA duties, like Skinner & Baddiel?

parts.note: co- is the prefix for joint or shared, as in co-host
public address work is done at a microphone, a mic

explanation.surface: Two presenters split the job of public announcements, like the well-known double act.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank Skinner and David Baddiel are British comedians who co-hosted TV shows, so sharing the mic fits them.
explanation.definitionFit: The pair are comedians, so they are funny performers in the adjectival sense.

clue.text: Hanger-on not extremely happy with closing time

indicators.note: not extremely says the outer letters of the word are dropped

parts.note: a closing is an end
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A clinging companion is far from overjoyed when the pub calls last orders.
explanation.walkthrough: Closing time is when British pubs stop serving.
explanation.definitionFit: Something attached to and hanging from a larger body is an appendage, a literal sense of the phrase.

clue.text: See 2
Creation of R Smythe Fitzgerald's voice only?

parts.note: Reg Smythe drew the British cartoon character Andy Capp, A. Capp
Ella Fitzgerald was the American jazz singer

explanation.surface: A cartoonist's creation is credited with Fitzgerald's voice and nothing else.
explanation.walkthrough: Andy Capp is a long-running British newspaper strip about a work-shy northerner; the apostrophe-s is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Singing without instrumental backing uses voices alone, the meaning of this musical term.

clue.text: Like old people on film?

definitions.meaning: belonging to the ancient civilisation of Peru
a finished movie is said to be 'in the can', so split 2,3 the word describes footage already shot

explanation.surface: A question of whether elderly folk resemble the way they appear on screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old people' is not the elderly but an ancient civilisation of Peru.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things belonging to the pre-Columbian empire of the Andes, an ancient nation.

clue.text: ____ to catch a deer, ____?

indicators.note: the second gap holds the French for 'that is to say', which tells the solver how the gap is spoken

parts.note: the proverb set a thief to catch a thief, applied to a deer, has 'set a deer' in the gap

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blanks riff on 'set a thief to catch a thief', applied to deer.
explanation.walkthrough: The French phrase means 'that is to say', and it sounds like 'set a deer', so it fills both gaps and also signals that the first is spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: The French expression introduces a restatement, an equivalent of 'in other words'.

clue.text: I take over Very Grand First Ballet

indicators.note: First says the piece before it leads the whole word

parts.note: K, from kilo, is slang for a grand, a thousand
R is the abbreviation for recipe, Latin for take
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: Someone claims to be taking over a grand premiere of a ballet.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kirov is the St Petersburg ballet company, now the Mariinsky.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kirov is a famous Russian ballet company, an example of the art form's troupes.

clue.text: Dear me!

parts.note: the exclamation of dismay read as the salutation of a letter written to oneself names its recipient

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear me!' sounds like mild dismay, but it is how a letter to yourself would open, making you its recipient.
explanation.definitionFit: The person a letter begins by naming is the one it is sent to.

clue.text: Provoke villain at back of home

indicators.note: at back of says the scoundrel word comes after the home word

parts.note: in means at home
a cur is a contemptible scoundrel

explanation.surface: A rogue lurking behind a house stirs up trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring on something unwelcome, such as anger or a penalty, is to provoke it, a close synonym.

clue.text: It's beastly modest, turning up

parts.note: coy means modest or shy

indicators.note: turning says the little word is flipped end to end

explanation.surface: Someone shy who suddenly appears is described as horrible.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'turning up' looks like 'arriving'; it is UP read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The coypu is a large South American water rodent, so it is a beast.

clue.text: In Hibernian's face, sharp Hearts get going in the cold

indicators.note: In says the card letter is placed within the face word

parts.note: puss is Irish slang for the face or mouth, Hibernian meaning Irish
H is the abbreviation for hearts in card games
tart means sharp in taste

explanation.surface: A football clash in which Edinburgh rivals Hibernian and Hearts get stuck in on a cold day.
explanation.walkthrough: Hibernian and Hearts are rival Edinburgh football clubs; here 'Hibernian' just means Irish.
explanation.definitionFit: A car whose battery fails in cold weather is started by being pushed, getting it running.

clue.text: Presumably you don't know if you do it

definitions.text: Presumably you don't know if you do it

parts.words: Presumably you don't know if you do it
parts.note: lifting the shoulders is the gesture of someone who has no idea

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a riddle about something done unawares; it means the gesture you make when you don't know.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising one's shoulders signals ignorance or indifference.

clue.text: See 5
Who makes lines most prominent in walks (both directions) weaving through nearly all of Dales?

definitions.text: Who makes lines most prominent in walks (both directions) weaving through nearly all of Dales?

indicators.note: weaving through says the pieces are threaded into the shortened word
nearly all of says the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: RY is the abbreviation for railway, lines of track

indicators.note: most prominent in picks the leading letter of the word that follows

parts.note: L and R stand for left and right, the two directions

explanation.surface: A walker in the Yorkshire Dales notices who builds the stone walls that line the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are threaded in through DALE separately: RY and W after D, L after AL, R at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A drystone waller builds field boundaries without mortar, making the lines of walls across the Dales.

clue.text: Hood is The Poet in Residence!

indicators.note: in Residence says the word lives within the run of letters in front of it

explanation.surface: Thomas Hood is declared the writer-in-residence.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hood was an English poet, which makes the clue look like a statement about him.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of odes is a poet, a crossword-favourite word for a versifier.

clue.text: Not usually England's lay, rendered about the middle of January

definitions.text: Not usually England's lay, rendered about the middle of January

indicators.note: about says the reworked letters go around the central letter
rendered says the song's letters are performed in a new arrangement
the middle of picks the central letter of the month

explanation.surface: A song not usually associated with England is performed around mid-January.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition shares 'England's lay' with the fodder: the song is Scottish, sung at New Year.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns's song is Scotland's New Year anthem, so it is seldom regarded as English.
